claim: The segmentation clock is visible as tissue-level kinematic waves of gene expression that travel through the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) and arrest at the position of each forming segment.
source: The clock is visible as tissue-level kinematic waves of gene expression that travel through the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) and arrest at the position of each forming segment.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations to prior work on wave patterns in the segmentation clock.

claim: Cell-extrinsic signals are not required by PSM cells to instruct the developmental program underlying the wave pattern.
source: This shows that cell-extrinsic signals are not required by the cells to instruct the developmental program underlying the wave pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cultured single PSM cells showing autonomous oscillatory and arrest dynamics.

claim: A cell-autonomous timing activity initiates during cell exit from the tailbud and runs down in the anterior-ward cell flow in the PSM.
source: We show that a cell-autonomous timing activity initiates during cell exit from the tailbud, then runs down in the anterior-ward cell flow in the PSM, thereby using elapsed time to provide positional information to the clock.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cells from different anteroposterior positions and tracking cells from tailbud to PSM.

claim: Exogenous FGF lengthens the duration of the cell-intrinsic timer.
source: Exogenous FGF lengthens the duration of the cell-intrinsic timer, indicating extrinsic factors in the embryo may regulate the segmentation clock via the timer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that FGF8 addition to culture medium extends the cell-autonomous program.

claim: A noisy cell-autonomous, intrinsic timer drives the slowing and arrest of oscillations underlying the wave pattern.
source: In sum, our work suggests that a noisy cell-autonomous, intrinsic timer drives the slowing and arrest of oscillations underlying the wave pattern, while extrinsic factors in the embryo tune this timer's duration and precision.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased variability in cultured cells compared to embryonic cells.

claim: Extrinsic factors in the embryo tune the timer's duration and precision.
source: In sum, our work suggests that a noisy cell-autonomous, intrinsic timer drives the slowing and arrest of oscillations underlying the wave pattern, while extrinsic factors in the embryo tune this timer's duration and precision.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dynamics in culture versus in the embryo, showing differences in duration and precision.

claim: Waves are produced by the slowing of oscillations in cells as they mature and flow anteriorly through the spatial reference frame of the PSM.
source: Waves are produced by the slowing of oscillations in cells as they mature and flow anteriorly through the spatial reference frame of the PSM; this slowing creates a phase shift along the anteroposterior axis (Delaune et al., 2012; Morelli et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2015; Yoshioka-Kobayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous work has implicated both cell-intrinsic mechanisms and extrinsic signals in driving the slowing of oscillations and clock arrest.
source: Previous work has implicated both cell-intrinsic mechanisms and extrinsic signals in driving the slowing of oscillations and clock arrest. These mechanisms include morphogen signaling gradients across the PSM (Ishimatsu et al., 2010, Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Moreno and Kintner, 2004; Sawada et al., 2001; Simsek and Özbudak, 2018), the decay of signaling factors carried anteriorly by PSM cells (Aulehla et al., 2003; Dubrulle and Pourquié, 2004), the counting of oscillations (Palmeirim et al., 1997; Zákány et al., 2001), the comparison of oscillators' phases within cells (Sonnen et al., 2018), and neighboring cells comparing their oscillations (Boareto et al., 2021; Murray et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Isolated PSM cells have been shown to autonomously oscillate in various permissive culture conditions.
source: Isolated PSM cells have been shown to autonomously oscillate in various permissive culture conditions (Oates, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Isolated human and mouse PSM cells derived from stem cells showed autonomous, sustained oscillations upon inhibition of YAP signaling.
source: Isolated human and mouse PSM cells derived from stem cells showed autonomous, sustained oscillations upon inhibition of YAP signaling (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Matsuda et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Primary PSM cells from mouse showed sustained oscillations upon either YAP signaling inhibition or use of a BSA-coated substrate.
source: Similarly, primary PSM cells from mouse showed sustained oscillations upon either YAP signaling inhibition (Hubaud et al., 2017; Yoshioka-Kobayashi et al., 2020) or use of a BSA-coated substrate (Hubaud et al., 2017), and zebrafish primary PSM cells exhibited sustained noisy oscillations upon addition of FGF8 (Webb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Zebrafish primary PSM cells exhibited sustained noisy oscillations upon addition of FGF8.
source: Similarly, primary PSM cells from mouse showed sustained oscillations upon either YAP signaling inhibition (Hubaud et al., 2017; Yoshioka-Kobayashi et al., 2020) or use of a BSA-coated substrate (Hubaud et al., 2017), and zebrafish primary PSM cells exhibited sustained noisy oscillations upon addition of FGF8 (Webb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In none of the previous cases was an oscillatory pattern observed for isolated cells that resembled the slowing frequency profile expected to underlie the in vivo wave pattern.
source: In none of these cases, however, was an oscillatory pattern observed for isolated cells that resembled the slowing frequency profile expected to underlie the in vivo wave pattern.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of prior literature.

claim: Transient (non-steady-state) oscillations were reported in zebrafish primary PSM cells cultured without signaling molecules, small molecule inhibitors, serum, or BSA.
source: Recently, we reported transient (non-steady-state) oscillations in zebrafish primary PSM cells cultured without signaling molecules, small molecule inhibitors, serum, or BSA (Negrete et al., 2021), yet it remains unclear how these oscillations relate to the wave pattern in the embryo.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Single PSM4 cells in culture produced Her1-YFP oscillations with 1–8 peaks before arresting.
source: Single PSM4 cells in culture produced Her1-YFP oscillations with 1–8 peaks before arresting (N=11 embryos, n=174 cells; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Oscillations in cultured PSM4 cells typically slowed then abruptly arrested.
source: These oscillations typically slowed then abruptly arrested (Figure 1D and F; Figure 1—figure supplements 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Oscillation arrest in cultured PSM4 cells was associated with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset.
source: Oscillation arrest, marked by the last Her1-YFP peak, was also associated with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset (Figure 1A and D), suggesting that arrest occurs in concert with differentiation as expected from the tissue-level pattern.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and D.

claim: The transient dynamics in cultured PSM4 cells were independent of cell-survival time in culture.
source: These transient dynamics were independent of cell-survival time in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), reproduced in cells isolated one-per-well (Figure 1—figure supplement 8) and did not require Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The transient dynamics in cultured PSM4 cells were reproduced in cells isolated one-per-well.
source: These transient dynamics were independent of cell-survival time in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), reproduced in cells isolated one-per-well (Figure 1—figure supplement 8) and did not require Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The transient dynamics in cultured PSM4 cells did not require Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2).
source: These transient dynamics were independent of cell-survival time in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), reproduced in cells isolated one-per-well (Figure 1—figure supplement 8) and did not require Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: The overall variation in arrest timing was not due to differences between the individual embryos or experiments.
source: Despite inevitable uncertainty in the exact A/P boundaries of the explanted PSM4 due to manual dissection, the overall variation in arrest timing was not due to differences between the individual embryos or experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 10), thus limiting its source to heterogeneity within the starting PSM4 cell population and/or to the noise in an intrinsic process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10.

claim: PSM4 cells autonomously slow oscillations and arrest the clock in concert with expression of a segmental differentiation marker.
source: Taken together, our data show that PSM4 cells autonomously slow oscillations and arrest the clock in concert with expression of a segmental differentiation marker.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Cells from the PSM4 region predominantly contributed to two of four somites.
source: Retaining their initial local anteroposterior arrangement, cells from the PSM4 region predominantly contributed to two of four somites and differed by at most one Her1-YFP peak within a somite (N=2 embryos, n=128 cells; Figure 1G and H; Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell tracking in embryos shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Cells from the PSM4 region differed by at most one Her1-YFP peak within a somite.
source: Retaining their initial local anteroposterior arrangement, cells from the PSM4 region predominantly contributed to two of four somites and differed by at most one Her1-YFP peak within a somite (N=2 embryos, n=128 cells; Figure 1G and H; Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell tracking in embryos shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Cells in culture produced on average more peaks than cells in the embryo (mean ± SD = 4.4±1.6 peaks in culture vs 3.4±1.0 peaks in the embryo).
source: Cells in culture produced on average more peaks and showed increased variability in the number of peaks compared to cells in the embryo (mean ± SD = 4.4±1.6 peaks in culture, COV 0.36; 3.4±1.0 peaks in the embryo, COV 0.29; Figure 1E,I), indicating a longer and more variable duration of the cell-autonomous transient dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cultured cells and embryonic cells shown in Figure 1E and I.

claim: Cells in culture showed increased variability in the number of peaks compared to cells in the embryo (COV 0.36 in culture vs COV 0.29 in the embryo).
source: Cells in culture produced on average more peaks and showed increased variability in the number of peaks compared to cells in the embryo (mean ± SD = 4.4±1.6 peaks in culture, COV 0.36; 3.4±1.0 peaks in the embryo, COV 0.29; Figure 1E,I), indicating a longer and more variable duration of the cell-autonomous transient dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cultured cells and embryonic cells shown in Figure 1E and I.

claim: The variability in culture is not due to a difference in initial heterogeneity within the cell population, but reflects an increase in the noise of the cell-autonomous dynamics.
source: Because the cells tracked in the embryo originated from the same starting population as those in culture, these results suggest that the variability in culture is not due to a difference in initial heterogeneity within that cell population, but reflects an increase in the noise of the cell-autonomous dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of cultured and embryonic cells from the same starting population.

claim: The key dynamic of successive period slowing was shared between PSM4 cells in culture and in the embryo (81% of successive cycles slowed in culture vs 79% in the embryo).
source: The key dynamic of successive period slowing was shared between PSM4 cells in culture and in the embryo (81% of successive cycles slowed in culture vs 79% in the embryo; Figure 1F and J; Figure 1—figure supplement 13C and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cultured and embryonic cells shown in Figure 1F and J.

claim: A rise in intensity from one peak to the next was seen less often in culture (72% successive cycles in culture) than in the embryo (92%).
source: However, a rise in intensity from one peak to the next was seen less often in culture (72% successive cycles in culture and 92% in the embryo; Figure 1F and J; Figure 1—figure supplement 13B and D), and there was less of a correlation between intensity rise and slowing in the culture than in the embryo (57% of successive cycles both slow and rise in culture vs 73% in the embryo; Figure 1F and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cultured and embryonic cells shown in Figure 1F and J.

claim: There was less of a correlation between intensity rise and slowing in culture (57%) than in the embryo (73%).
source: However, a rise in intensity from one peak to the next was seen less often in culture (72% successive cycles in culture and 92% in the embryo; Figure 1F and J; Figure 1—figure supplement 13B and D), and there was less of a correlation between intensity rise and slowing in the culture than in the embryo (57% of successive cycles both slow and rise in culture vs 73% in the embryo; Figure 1F and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cultured and embryonic cells shown in Figure 1F and J.

claim: Although the cell-autonomous program generates slowing oscillations, the amplitude of the oscillations is noisier, suggesting that this feature may be tuned by extrinsic factors in the tissue.
source: These differences in accompanying intensity rise show that although the cell-autonomous program generates slowing oscillations, the amplitude of the oscillations is noisier, suggesting that this feature may be tuned by extrinsic factors in the tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of amplitude dynamics in culture versus embryo.

claim: All cells in the somite expressed Her1-YFP.
source: All cells in the somite expressed Her1-YFP and most produced a last peak in the prospective somite (S –1), creating a phase profile across the future rostral-caudal somite axis that reflected the tissue-level wave's arrival (n=233 cells, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from backtracking cells in the embryo shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Most cells in the somite produced a last Her1-YFP peak in the prospective somite (S-1).
source: All cells in the somite expressed Her1-YFP and most produced a last peak in the prospective somite (S –1), creating a phase profile across the future rostral-caudal somite axis that reflected the tissue-level wave's arrival (n=233 cells, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from backtracking cells in the embryo shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: In the embryo, clock arrest of all the cells that form a single somite does not occur simultaneously, but is spatiotemporally limited within S-1.
source: Thus, in the embryo, clock arrest of all the cells that form a single somite does not occur simultaneously, but is nevertheless spatiotemporally limited within S-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of last peak timing across cells in the somite.

claim: Most PSM4 cells in culture that survived past 5 hr and remained undivided were found to oscillate and arrest Her1-YFP.
source: Similar to the embryo, most PSM4 cells in culture that survived past 5 hr and remained undivided were found to oscillate and arrest Her1-YFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mesp-ba-mKate2 was first detected within the forming somite (S0), with higher levels rostrally.
source: Mesp-ba-mKate2 was first detected within the forming somite (S0), with higher levels rostrally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of Mesp-ba-mKate2 expression patterns.

claim: The distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity rise and proportion of cells with a clear signal-onset time in the embryo was comparable to that seen within the PSM4 cells in culture.
source: The distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity rise and proportion of cells with a clear signal-onset time in the embryo was comparable to that seen within the PSM4 cells in culture (N=2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that there is no cell-autonomous default state of Mesp 'on' or 'off'.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There is no cell-autonomous default state of Mesp 'on' or 'off'.
source: The distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity rise and proportion of cells with a clear signal-onset time in the embryo was comparable to that seen within the PSM4 cells in culture (N=2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that there is no cell-autonomous default state of Mesp 'on' or 'off'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset in culture and embryo.

claim: Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset mostly occurred after the last Her1-YFP peak in the embryo.
source: We found that Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset mostly occurred after the last Her1-YFP peak in the embryo. However, this relationship was not as precise in culture, with Mesp-ba-mKate signal-onset spanning the last peak (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), indicating a loss of coordination in the transition between clock arrest and segment polarization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The relationship between Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset and Her1-YFP last peak was not as precise in culture as in the embryo, indicating a loss of coordination in the transition between clock arrest and segment polarization.
source: We found that Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset mostly occurred after the last Her1-YFP peak in the embryo. However, this relationship was not as precise in culture, with Mesp-ba-mKate signal-onset spanning the last peak (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), indicating a loss of coordination in the transition between clock arrest and segment polarization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: A similar proportion of Mesp signal-onset was detected in control Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) and her1-/-; her7-/-; Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) cells.
source: We detected a similar proportion of Mesp signal-onset in control Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) and her1-/-; her7-/-; Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), and observed comparable timing (281±62 min in control cells, 305±70 min in her1-/-; her7-/- cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The timing of Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset was comparable in control cells (281±62 min) and her1-/-; her7-/- cells (305±70 min).
source: We detected a similar proportion of Mesp signal-onset in control Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) and her1-/-; her7-/-; Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), and observed comparable timing (281±62 min in control cells, 305±70 min in her1-/-; her7-/- cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The timing of Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset appears independent of the segmentation clock's oscillations.
source: Thus, the timing of Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset appears independent of the segmentation clock's oscillations, suggesting that timing information that feeds into both the clock and differentiation across the PSM does not require clock oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mesp signal-onset timing is similar in cells with and without functional clock oscillations.

claim: Timing information that feeds into both the clock and differentiation across the PSM does not require clock oscillations.
source: Thus, the timing of Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset appears independent of the segmentation clock's oscillations, suggesting that timing information that feeds into both the clock and differentiation across the PSM does not require clock oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mesp signal-onset timing is similar in cells with and without functional clock oscillations.

claim: The slowing and arrest of oscillations underlying the wave pattern in embryos is driven cell-autonomously in differentiating PSM cells.
source: Together, our data suggests that the slowing and arrest of oscillations underlying the wave pattern in embryos is driven cell-autonomously in differentiating PSM cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The noisier dynamics of the cell-autonomous program suggest that extrinsic signals present in the embryo may adjust the time of clock arrest in concert with differentiation, and sharpen clock oscillatory dynamics.
source: However, the noisier dynamics of the cell-autonomous program suggest that extrinsic signals present in the embryo may adjust the time of clock arrest in concert with differentiation, and sharpen clock oscillatory dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dynamics in culture versus embryo.

claim: A gradient of FGF signaling has been shown to extend from the tailbud across the PSM.
source: A gradient of FGF signaling has been shown to extend from the tailbud across the PSM and has been postulated to provide spatiotemporal information to the segmentation clock (Akiyama et al., 2014; Dubrulle and Pourquié, 2004; Sari et al., 2018; Sawada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FGF signaling has been postulated to provide spatiotemporal information to the segmentation clock.
source: A gradient of FGF signaling has been shown to extend from the tailbud across the PSM and has been postulated to provide spatiotemporal information to the segmentation clock (Akiyama et al., 2014; Dubrulle and Pourquié, 2004; Sari et al., 2018; Sawada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous experiments implanting FGF8-soaked beads adjacent to posterior PSM in the embryo resulted in an extension of clock/PSM activity such that somite boundary formation was delayed, yielding shorter segments.
source: Previous experiments implanting FGF8-soaked beads adjacent to posterior PSM in the embryo resulted in an extension of clock/PSM activity such that somite boundary formation was delayed, yielding shorter segments (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Addition of FGF8 to the culture medium extended the cell-autonomous program in PSM4 cells, increasing the mean number of oscillations generated per cell.
source: Consistent with this delay in the embryo, we found that addition of FGF8 to the culture medium extended the cell-autonomous program in PSM4 cells, increasing the mean number of oscillations generated per cell (Figure 3C) and shifting the Her1-YFP last peak to later times (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Addition of FGF8 to the culture medium shifted the Her1-YFP last peak to later times in PSM4 cells.
source: Consistent with this delay in the embryo, we found that addition of FGF8 to the culture medium extended the cell-autonomous program in PSM4 cells, increasing the mean number of oscillations generated per cell (Figure 3C) and shifting the Her1-YFP last peak to later times (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Exogenous FGF did not reduce noise in the cell-autonomous program.
source: Notably, exogenous FGF did not reduce noise in the cell-autonomous program (Figure 3C and D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Despite the Her1-YFP last peak occurring later on average with FGF treatment, it retained a temporal association with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset.
source: Despite the Her1-YFP last peak occurring later on average, it retained a temporal association with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset in the presence of FGF (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and the distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity traces was not altered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity traces was not altered by FGF treatment.
source: Despite the Her1-YFP last peak occurring later on average, it retained a temporal association with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset in the presence of FGF (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and the distribution of Mesp-ba-mKate2 intensity traces was not altered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A small subset of FGF-treated cells (5 out of 54 cells) produced multiple Her1-YFP oscillations after the Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset.
source: Interestingly, a small subset of cells (5 out of 54 cells) produced multiple Her1-YFP oscillations after the Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these events can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clock arrest and Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset can be uncoupled.
source: Interestingly, a small subset of cells (5 out of 54 cells) produced multiple Her1-YFP oscillations after the Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these events can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some cells oscillate after Mesp signal-onset.

claim: PSM4 can cell-autonomously extend the timing of clock arrest and segmental differentiation in response to FGF.
source: Together, these results indicate that PSM4 can cell-autonomously extend the timing of clock arrest and segmental differentiation in response to FGF.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data with FGF treatment.

claim: Successive oscillations continued to slow overall in the presence of FGF, although in fewer successive cycles (65% in FGF-treated cells vs 81% in control).
source: We found that successive oscillations continued to slow overall in the presence of FGF, although in fewer successive cycles (65% in FGF-treated cells vs 81% in control; Figure 3E and F), suggesting some disorganization of the dynamics in the FGF-extended cell-autonomous program.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: FGF treatment suggests some disorganization of the dynamics in the cell-autonomous program.
source: We found that successive oscillations continued to slow overall in the presence of FGF, although in fewer successive cycles (65% in FGF-treated cells vs 81% in control; Figure 3E and F), suggesting some disorganization of the dynamics in the FGF-extended cell-autonomous program.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of reduced frequency of successive slowing with FGF.

claim: Successive increase in peak intensity was observed in FGF-treated cells (66%) compared to control (73%), mostly in conjunction with slowing oscillations.
source: Successive increase in peak intensity was also observed (66% of FGF-treated cells vs 73% of control; Figure 3E and G), mostly in conjunction with slowing oscillations (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Despite increased noise in the cell-autonomous program with FGF, there was no systematic alteration of the period and intensity.
source: Despite this increased noise in the cell-autonomous program, we did not observe a systematic alteration of the period and intensity in response to FGF (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: FGF extends the duration of the cell-autonomous program transient dynamics in a manner that could explain reported effects of FGF activity on segment boundary position in the embryo.
source: Together, our data shows that FGF extends the duration of the cell-autonomous program transient dynamics in a manner that could explain reported effects of FGF activity on segment boundary position in the embryo (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2001) and supports a hypothesis that extrinsic signals act upon the clock through the cell-autonomous program.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data with FGF treatment and citations to prior work.

claim: Extrinsic signals act upon the clock through the cell-autonomous program.
source: Together, our data shows that FGF extends the duration of the cell-autonomous program transient dynamics in a manner that could explain reported effects of FGF activity on segment boundary position in the embryo (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2001) and supports a hypothesis that extrinsic signals act upon the clock through the cell-autonomous program.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the experimental data with FGF treatment.

claim: Isolated PSM cells originating more anteriorly successively slowed oscillations, but tended to produce fewer peaks than PSM4 cells and arrested Her1-YFP earlier in concert with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset.
source: Consistent with a timer running down in the embryo, isolated PSM cells originating more anteriorly successively slowed oscillations, but tended to produced fewer peaks than PSM4 cells and arrested Her1-YFP earlier in concert with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset (Figure 4B–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E; Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cells from different anteroposterior positions shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: Single TB cells in culture oscillated with successive slowing, then arrested concurrent with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset.
source: We found that single TB cells in culture oscillated with successive slowing, then arrested concurrent with Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal-onset (Figure 4B–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cultured TB cells shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: TB and PSM4 dissected from the same embryos were found to arrest oscillations with similar timing, despite the more posterior origin of the TB cells.
source: Moreover, TB and PSM4 dissected from the same embryos were found to arrest oscillations with similar timing, despite the more posterior origin of the TB cells (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing TB and PSM4 cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Experimental removal from the TB starts the intrinsic timer such that its duration is equivalent to that of cells which have recently entered the PSM.
source: These results suggest that experimental removal from the TB starts the intrinsic timer such that its duration is equivalent to that of cells which have recently entered the PSM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TB and PSM4 cells arrest with similar timing.

claim: TB cells have already expressed the cell-autonomous timing mechanism, but require a trigger associated with exit from the TB to start the timing activity.
source: We thus propose that TB cells have already expressed the cell-autonomous timing mechanism, but require a trigger associated with exit from the TB to start the timing activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that TB cells arrest with similar timing to PSM4 cells when cultured.

claim: Cells within the TB are known to mix and remain for a range of times before joining the PSM.
source: Cells within the TB are known to mix and remain for a range of times before joining the PSM (Mara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: While in the TB, individual cells from both groups showed low-intensity, noisy Her1-YFP oscillations.
source: We observed that while in the TB, individual cells from both groups showed low-intensity, noisy Her1-YFP oscillations (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TB cells that will later become PSM in the zebrafish do oscillate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from backtracking cells in the embryo shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: TB cells that will later become PSM in the zebrafish do oscillate.
source: We observed that while in the TB, individual cells from both groups showed low-intensity, noisy Her1-YFP oscillations (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TB cells that will later become PSM in the zebrafish do oscillate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from backtracking cells in the embryo shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: As cells exited the TB and joined the PSM, their oscillations slowed successively and increased in peak intensity.
source: As the embryo developed, the group of cells backtracked from the recently formed somite were the first to join the PSM, at which time their oscillations slowed successively and increased in peak intensity (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from backtracking cells in the embryo shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: The tight correlation of the initiation of slowing oscillations in cells with their exit from the TB in the embryo supports the idea that exit from the TB starts the intrinsic timer.
source: This tight correlation of the initiation of slowing oscillations in cells with their exit from the TB in the embryo supports the idea that exit from the TB starts the intrinsic timer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that slowing oscillations begin when cells exit the TB.

claim: The role of short-range cell-cell signaling through the Delta-Notch pathway in the local synchronization of the oscillators is well established.
source: The role of short-range cell-cell signaling through the Delta-Notch pathway in the local synchronization of the oscillators is well established (Venzin and Oates, 2020), providing local coherence to the wave pattern.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The results clearly implicate a cell-autonomous program of slowing and stopping as the basis for the tissue-level wave-pattern in the zebrafish.
source: Our results clearly implicate a cell-autonomous program of slowing and stopping as the basis for the tissue-level wave-pattern in the zebrafish, and show that a universal picture of the vertebrate segmentation clock that is centered on persistent cellular oscillators instructed by extrinsic signals is inadequate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: A universal picture of the vertebrate segmentation clock that is centered on persistent cellular oscillators instructed by extrinsic signals is inadequate.
source: Our results clearly implicate a cell-autonomous program of slowing and stopping as the basis for the tissue-level wave-pattern in the zebrafish, and show that a universal picture of the vertebrate segmentation clock that is centered on persistent cellular oscillators instructed by extrinsic signals is inadequate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing cell-autonomous dynamics.

claim: The work highlights the importance of transient dynamics driven by a cell-autonomous timing mechanism.
source: Rather, our work highlights the importance of transient dynamics driven by a cell-autonomous timing mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: The concept of a cell-intrinsic timer explains the long-known intrinsic properties of explanted PSM tissue from several species to segment with periodicity and AP directionality.
source: However, the concept of a cell-intrinsic timer explains the long-known intrinsic properties of explanted PSM tissue from several species to segment with periodicity and AP directionality (Aulehla and Pourquié, 2006; Dubrulle et al., 2001; Henry et al., 2005; Lauschke et al., 2013; Maroto et al., 2005; Palmeirim et al., 1997; Palmeirim et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on explanted PSM tissue.

claim: The 'Clock and Wavefront' model originally postulated an intracellular timing gradient as the mechanism behind the wavefront of cellular change interacting with the clock to determine somite position.
source: Indeed, the long-standing 'Clock and Wavefront' model of the segmentation clock originally postulated an intracellular timing gradient as the mechanism behind the wavefront of cellular change interacting with the clock to determine somite position (Cooke and Zeeman, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original Clock and Wavefront model.

claim: Both the clock and the wavefront, comprising an intracellular timing mechanism, are captured in a single cell running an autonomous program.
source: Here, we have shown that both the clock and the wavefront, comprising just such an intracellular timing mechanism, are captured in a single cell running an autonomous program.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In cells treated by FGF, the timing of arrest of oscillations and the onset of differentiation were dissociated in approximately 10% of cells.
source: Curiously, we observed that in cells treated by FGF, the timing of arrest of oscillations and the onset of differentiation were dissociated in approximately 10% of cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from FGF-treated cells.

claim: There may be two (or more) parallel timing mechanisms underlying the normal tight linkage of clock arrest and differentiation.
source: One interpretation of this result is that there are two (or more) parallel timing mechanisms underlying the normal tight linkage of clock arrest and differentiation, and elevated FGF signaling can cause these mechanisms to uncouple in a small set of cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that clock arrest and differentiation can be dissociated.

claim: The clock arrest and onset of differentiation may use different sensors of the same timer.
source: Another interpretation is that the clock arrest and onset of differentiation use different sensors of the same timer. Although these sensors react closely in time under normal circumstances, with a change in the timer's dynamics caused by FGF (e.g. a lower slope of a timing gradient) the sensors react at different times in a small set of cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that clock arrest and differentiation can be dissociated.

claim: A similar dissociation of clock arrest and differentiation timing has previously been inferred in the doppelkorn medaka mutant from gene expression patterns.
source: A similar dissociation of clock arrest and differentiation timing has previously been inferred in the doppelkorn medaka mutant from gene expression patterns (Elmasri et al., 2004), suggesting the doppelkorn gene, when identified, may shed further light on the phenomenon.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on the doppelkorn mutant.

claim: The difference in duration and precision between cellular dynamics in the embryo and those in culture conditions distinguishes important roles of extrinsic signaling in the zebrafish segmentation clock.
source: The difference in duration and precision between cellular dynamics in the embryo and those in culture conditions distinguishes important roles of extrinsic signaling in the zebrafish segmentation clock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dynamics in culture versus embryo.

claim: The roles of extrinsic signaling are to regulate the length of the autonomous program and to increase the precision of the exit time in the population.
source: These roles are to regulate the length of the autonomous program and to increase the precision of the exit time in the population, so that all cells contributing to a single somite in the embryo stop oscillating within the period of somite formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dynamics in culture versus embryo.

claim: The ability of FGF to extend the duration of the program of cultured posterior PSM cells fits well with data from experiments in the embryo demonstrating that an increase or decrease in FGF activity can alter segment length.
source: The ability of FGF to extend the duration of the program of cultured posterior PSM cells fits well with data from experiments in the embryo demonstrating that an increase or decrease in FGF activity can alter segment length (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Sawada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with FGF treatment and citations to prior work.

claim: Despite the increased duration in culture with FGF, FGF did not reduce the variability of the dynamics, implying that additional signals, or temporal signaling dynamics, are important for precision at the tissue level.
source: Despite the increased duration in culture, FGF did not reduce the variability of the dynamics, implying that additional signals, or temporal signaling dynamics, are important for precision at the tissue level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that FGF extends duration but does not reduce variability.

claim: The rapid decrease of external signals required for maintenance of a stable oscillatory state, normally restricted to the tailbud, would explain the observed dynamics when cells exit the TB.
source: How the timer is triggered upon the exit of a cell from the tailbud to the PSM is likewise not known, but our experiments suggest that the rapid decrease of external signals required for maintenance of a stable oscillatory state (Hubaud and Pourquié, 2014), and normally restricted to the tailbud, would explain the observed dynamics.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the experimental observations and citation to prior work.

claim: The molecular details of the timer are not constrained by the data and could involve a number of plausible intermediates such as transcription factor or microRNA cascades or phospho-timers.
source: The molecular details of the timer are not constrained by our data here, and could involve a number of plausible intermediates such as transcription factor or microRNA cascades similar to those in timing of neuroblast differentiation or C. elegans molting (Ambros, 2011; Brody and Odenwald, 2000) or phospho-timers as found in the circadian clock (Diernfellner and Brunner, 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about possible molecular mechanisms, supported by citations to analogous systems.

claim: A phospho-timer mechanism would provide an attractive link to extrinsic signalling by FGF gradients in the PSM.
source: The latter mechanism would provide an attractive link to extrinsic signalling by FGF gradients in the PSM (Sawada et al., 2001; Simsek and Özbudak, 2018).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible molecular mechanism, supported by citations to prior work on FGF gradients.

claim: A model for slowing and then stopping oscillations via the rise and fall of Her1 production implies that molecules controlling her1 transcription, such as Tbx proteins and/or Her1 translation, are involved as time-keeping factors.
source: A model for slowing and then stopping oscillations via the rise and fall of Her1 production (Negrete et al., 2021) implies that molecules controlling her1 transcription, such as Tbx proteins (Brend and Holley, 2009) and/or Her1 translation (Dill and Amacher, 2005) are involved as time-keeping factors.
evidence: This is speculation about possible molecular mechanisms, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The activity of the Tbx-degrading factor Ripply may play a role in the threshold at which production falls, thereby rapidly stopping the oscillations.
source: In this light, the activity of the Tbx-degrading factor Ripply (Wanglar et al., 2014) may play a role in the threshold at which production falls, thereby rapidly stopping the oscillations.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible molecular mechanism, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Other models posit that the slowing of Her oscillations arise due to an increase of time-delays in the negative feedback loop of the core clock circuit.
source: Other models posit that the slowing of Her oscillations arise due to an increase of time-delays in the negative feedback loop of the core clock circuit (Ay et al., 2014; Yabe et al., 2023), suggesting that factors influencing the duration of pre-mRNA splicing, translation, or nuclear transport may be relevant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The timer exerts control over differentiation independent of the clock.
source: Whatever the identity, our results suggest that the timer exerts control over differentiation independent of the clock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mesp signal-onset timing is independent of clock oscillations.

claim: Understanding the cell-intrinsic potential within multicellular systems is vital to interpreting and directing population level behavior.
source: Although patterns in multicellular contexts can emerge from extrinsic signaling processes alone (Danino et al., 2010), understanding the cell-intrinsic potential within these various systems is vital to interpreting and directing population level behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citation to prior work and the findings of this study.

claim: The work combining isolated primary cell culture and single-cell resolution imaging of the corresponding developing tissue reveals that cell-autonomous timing directs the tissue-level patterning of the clock.
source: Our work combining isolated primary cell culture and single-cell resolution imaging of the corresponding developing tissue, reveals that cell-autonomous timing directs the tissue-level patterning of the clock, and offers new opportunities to study the balance of extrinsic and intrinsic control in oscillatory patterning systems.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental approach and findings.

claim: mesp-ba-mKate2 mRNA was detected only in the rostral half of pre-segments (S–II and S–I) in the anterior PSM as expected from endogenous mesp-ba expression.
source: mesp-ba-mKate2 was detected only in the rostral half of pre-segments (S–II and S–I) in the anterior PSM as expected from endogenous mesp-ba expression (Cutty et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to prior work.

claim: Mesp-ba-mKate2 was first detected by antibodies to mKate2 in the rostral half of S-I, where it persisted in the newly forming somite (S0) and formed somites (SI).
source: Mesp-ba-mKate2 was first detected by antibodies to mKate2 in the rostral half of S-I, where it persisted in the newly forming somite (S0) and formed somites (SI).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal was first detected in live Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) embryos within the rostral half of S0, after which it remained in the rostral half of the formed somites.
source: Mesp-ba-mKate2 signal was first detected in live Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) embryos within the rostral half of S0 (*), after which it remained in the rostral half of the formed somites (21 somite-stage embryo).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Boundary formation was normal in Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) embryos compared to wildtype as detected by in situ hybridization for the boundary marker xirp2a at 2 days post-fertilization.
source: Boundary formation was normal as detected by in situ hybridization for the boundary marker xirp2a in Tg(mesp-ba-mKate2) embryos compared to wildtype (WT) at 2 days post-fertilization (dpf).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
